title: New Dementia Cases Could More than Double by 2050
paragraphs: New research suggests that the number of people developing dementia each year could more than double by 2050.
Dementia already affects millions of people around the world. According to the World Health Organization, 57 million people worldwide were living with the condition in 2021.

And the number of new cases is expected to rise sharply. Researchers at the University of New South Wales in Australia estimate that 11.4 million people around the world developed dementia in 2023. And by 2050, the number of new cases could reach 24.7 million a year.
The researchers studied data from more than 38,000 people in 18 countries to find out which groups were more likely to develop dementia.

They found that women had higher rates of dementia than men. There were also large differences between countries. In lower-income countries, about 14 out of every 1,000 people developed dementia each year, compared with about eight in every 1,000 in richer countries.

The researchers say more work is needed to understand why dementia rates differ between these groups, but they say the differences could be connected to people's health, education, living conditions and environment.
But the study also points out a problem with dementia research.
Much of the existing research on dementia has been carried out in higher-income countries, even though some of the largest increases are expected in poorer countries.
Perminder Sachdev, one of the study's researchers, said this is worrying because many of these poorer countries have aging populations but less money and fewer services to help people with dementia.
Henry Brodaty, another of the researchers, said governments need to do more than just care for people after they develop dementia.
He believes it's important to invest in dementia prevention and to find ways to identify people who are at risk before they develop it.
And with so many new cases expected, better prevention and care will be more important than ever.
